questions.title: How do you answer when asked about a required certification you do not yet hold?
questions.quick: I state the position plainly, then show the plan. I say I do not hold it yet, explain what the certification covers, and show the evidence of practical competence in those areas. Then I give a dated study plan, such as the exam booking and weekly schedule, and offer to share progress. I do not claim a pass that has not happened or play down the requirement. If it is mandatory, I confirm the timeline the employer expects and commit to it.
questions.revision: Be honest and brief about the gap, evidence the practical competence, give a dated plan with milestones, and confirm the employer deadline.
questions.detailed:
A certification question tests **honesty, self-management and judgement**. A short, confident, honest answer works better than defensiveness.

## A reusable structure

1. **State the position.** "I do not hold that certification yet."
2. **Show you understand it.** Name what the exam measures, in a sentence or two.
3. **Give evidence.** Point to concrete work that covers the same domains (designs, deliveries, incidents handled).
4. **Show the plan.** Exam date or target window, study resources, practice tests, weekly hours.
5. **Close on the requirement.** "If it is required within a set period, I will plan to that date."

## Template

"I do not hold [certification] yet. It covers [areas]. In my work I have [practical evidence for two or three areas]. I am preparing for it now: [resource], [weekly hours], with the exam planned for [window]. If the role needs it by a specific date, I can work to that."

## Weak versus strong

| Weak | Strong |
|---|---|
| "I am planning to take it sometime" | "Exam booked for [month]; practice scores are [verifiable]" |
| Listing every course taken | Linking each domain to real work |
| Criticising the certification | Respecting it while showing equal depth |
| Overclaiming ("practically certified") | Precise status |

## Handling a mandatory requirement

- Ask when the organisation expects it and whether it supports exam fees and study time.
- Offer interim evidence such as module completion or a practice assessment.
- Do not negotiate it away; show you will meet it.

## Common mistakes

- Hiding the gap and being found out later.
- Giving a vague timeline.
- Saying the certification does not matter.
- Listing study without any evidence of practice.
followUps: What if the interviewer says it must be done within a month?
How do you prove competence without the certificate?
How do you choose which exam to take first?

questions.title: How do you present transferable experience when a role lists a technology you have used only partly?
questions.quick: I name the depth honestly, then connect concepts. I say what I have used and to what level, map it to the listed technology through shared ideas such as identity, data modelling, deployment pipelines and integration, and explain where the differences lie. Then I give a learning plan with a first milestone, ideally a small build, and I show how quickly I have picked up similar tools before. I avoid pretending breadth I cannot back with a concrete example.
questions.revision: State depth precisely, map shared concepts, name real differences, show past fast learning, and commit to a concrete short learning plan with a first milestone.
questions.detailed:
Interviewers want to know whether you can **ramp up quickly without misrepresenting**. Precision about depth builds trust.

## A reusable structure

1. **Depth statement.** "I have used [part] for [duration or project]; I have not yet used [other part] in production."
2. **Concept mapping.** Show what carries over.
3. **Differences.** Name two or three things that work differently and how you would learn them.
4. **Evidence of ramping.** A previous case where you learned a new tool and delivered.
5. **Plan.** First two weeks: what you will read, build and ask.

## Concept mapping example (generic)

| Known area | Carries over to the new tool as |
|---|---|
| Role-based access in one platform | Security roles and scopes |
| Deployment pipelines in code | Environment promotion and packaging |
| REST integration and data modelling | Connectors, tables and relationships |
| Event-driven workflows | Triggers and flows |

## Template

"I have used [technology A] for [context], to the level of [depth]. The listed [technology B] shares [concepts]. The main differences I would expect are [x, y], and I would close those by [action]. When I moved to [earlier tool], I was productive within [timeframe] by [method]. For this role I would start with [small build] in the first two weeks."

## Depth vocabulary

- **Explored:** tutorials and prototypes.
- **Used:** built and delivered something real.
- **Operated:** run it in production, handled issues.
- **Designed:** made architecture decisions and trade-offs.

Use the right word each time.

## Common mistakes

- Claiming equivalence between concepts that are only similar.
- Over-apologising, which weakens a sound answer.
- Offering no plan.
- Using buzzwords without being able to explain them in detail.
followUps: How do you tell an interviewer where your knowledge ends?
What small build would prove you can ramp up in two weeks?
Which differences between similar platforms are most often underestimated?

questions.title: How do you structure a 90-second introduction for an engineering lead interview?
questions.quick: I use four beats: present, past, proof and purpose. Present is my current role and scope in one sentence. Past is the two or three experiences that shaped how I lead. Proof is one measurable outcome and how I led the team to it. Purpose is why this role and what I would do first. I rehearse it to about ninety seconds, keep numbers specific only where they are true, and end with a hook that invites a question.
questions.revision: Present, past, proof, purpose: current scope, shaping experience, one measurable outcome, why this role. About 220 words, with a closing hook.
questions.detailed:
Ninety seconds is roughly **200 to 230 spoken words**. The aim is to guide the interviewer to the topics you want to discuss.

## The four beats

| Beat | Time | Content |
|---|---|---|
| Present | 20 seconds | Role, team size, domain, what you are accountable for |
| Past | 25 seconds | Two or three experiences that built your leadership and technical base |
| Proof | 30 seconds | One outcome with context, your action, the result |
| Purpose | 15 seconds | Why this role, what you would focus on first |

{{diagram:intro}}

## Template with placeholders

"I currently lead [team size] engineers on [domain], responsible for [delivery, architecture, quality]. Before that I [past experience one] and [past experience two], which taught me [lesson about leading]. One example: [situation], where I [action], resulting in [measurable result, only if accurate]. I am interested in this role because [link to the role's needs], and in the first months I would focus on [priority one, priority two]. Happy to go deeper on [topic you want to be asked about]."

## Engineering lead specifics

- Include **people and delivery** as well as technology: how you coach, plan, and handle risk.
- Show both **breadth** (architecture, delivery) and **depth** in one area.
- Use plain language; avoid listing every tool.

## Practice routine

1. Write it, then speak it with a timer.
2. Cut adjectives, keep verbs and results.
3. Prepare a one-line version and a three-minute version.
4. Adapt the proof example to the job description.

## Common mistakes

- Reciting a career timeline year by year.
- Spending the whole time on the past.
- Using numbers you cannot defend.
- Ending without a hook, so the interviewer has no obvious next question.

diagrams.title: Ninety second introduction flow
diagrams.alt: The introduction moves from present role and scope to past experiences, then a single proof example with a result, then the purpose for the role, and ends with a hook that invites the interviewer to ask a follow-up question.

followUps: How do you adapt the proof example to different job descriptions?
How do you handle an interviewer who interrupts halfway?
